lessons.title: Grinding and batching
lessons.html:
Grinding and batching

Mixed feed production turns individual ingredients into a uniform blend that matches the nutritionist's formulation. Two steps come first: reducing particle size and weighing ingredients accurately.

Grinding

Grinding increases surface area, which improves digestibility and helps mixing and pelleting.

MillFeatures
Hammer millSwinging hammers shatter material against a screen; screen hole size controls fineness; versatile but uses more energy and makes more fines
Roller millGrain passes between rollers; more uniform particles, less dust and energy; less suited to fibrous material

The correct particle size depends on the species. Poultry often need a coarser grind than pigs, and pellet quality needs a reasonably fine grind. Follow the specification for each product. Check screens for holes every shift: a torn screen lets coarse particles through and changes the product. Magnets ahead of the mill protect the hammers and screens.

Batching

The batching system weighs each ingredient for a batch according to the formulation:

  • Major ingredients (maize, soya, wheat bran) are weighed on large hopper scales from production bins.
  • Minor ingredients (limestone, salt, monocalcium phosphate) on smaller scales.
  • Micro-ingredients (premixes, enzymes, amino acids, medicaments) on precision scales, often hand-added with a check.
  • Liquids (fat, oil, molasses) by meter or load cell.

Scale accuracy is critical. Scales are calibrated on a schedule and checked with test weights. Every batch record shows target and actual weights. Deviations outside tolerance must be stopped and reported, not corrected by guessing.

Common batching errors include an ingredient bin running empty, a bin containing the wrong material, a feeder gate that sticks open, and a hand-add that is forgotten or doubled. Most automated systems detect weight errors, but only careful operators detect a correct weight of the wrong material.

lessons.title: Mixing and preventing contamination
lessons.html:
Mixing and preventing contamination

Mixers

  • Horizontal ribbon or paddle mixers are the most common batch mixers. They mix quickly and allow liquid addition.
  • Vertical mixers are cheaper but slower and leave more residue.

Mixing time and sequence

Each mixer has a validated mixing time. Too short leaves an uneven mix; too long wastes time and can cause separation. A typical sequence is: majors in, then minors and micros, a dry mix, then liquids, then a wet mix, then discharge. Your mill's SOP sets the exact sequence and times.

Mix uniformity

A uniform mix means every mouthful contains the right nutrients. Mills test this by adding a tracer or measuring a nutrient in several samples from one batch and calculating the coefficient of variation (CV). A low CV means a uniform mix. The target CV is set by the mill's quality system. Poor results point to worn ribbons, overfilling, wrong mixing time or wrong addition sequence.

Carry-over and cross-contamination

Residue from one batch can end up in the next. This is dangerous when the previous batch contained medicaments or ingredients unsafe for some species, for example certain ionophores that are toxic to horses.

  • Follow the production sequence plan: non-medicated before medicated, sensitive species first.
  • Use flush batches (for example ground maize) where required and record them.
  • Keep mixers, screws and bins clean; check for build-up.
  • Use dedicated equipment for medicaments where possible.

Records

Batch records include formulation, ingredient lots, weights, mix times, operator and any deviations. They are the basis of traceability under feed registration and food safety systems.

Key points

  • Grinding sets particle size; check screens and magnets every shift.
  • Accurate, calibrated scales are essential for correct nutrition.
  • Follow validated mixing times and addition sequence.
  • Uniformity is measured by CV; a low CV means an even mix.
  • Sequence, flushing and cleaning control carry-over.
